newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan finance minister stakes all on growth.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan finance minister stakes all on growth.

text.p: Pakistan's new finance minister says only export-led growth can pull the country out of economic crisis after the collapse of another International Monetary Fund lending programme.

"Lasting improvement will come from increased production and productivity," Sartaj Aziz told Reuters in an interview on Saturday. "If you ask me what are our three priorities for the next three years, I will say exports, exports, exports."
He was speaking after an IMF mission left on Friday following talks on an $830 million standby loan, of which the remaining $370 million was due to have been disbursed by September.

Aziz said the IMF was discontinuing the loan because Pakistan had been unable to meet agreed targets, especially revenue measures designed to cut the 1996/97 (July-June) budget deficit to four percent of GDP from 6.3 percent in 1995/96.
The fund, he said, had agreed to start early talks on a medium-term structural adjustment loan (ESAF), once the government announces details of its economic policy.
Aziz said the standby programme's benefits would have been limited even if its terms had been carried out to the letter.

"If they are accompanied by a strong supply side response, and structural reforms in the taxation and tariff structure, and supported by institutional reforms and reduction in expenditure, the combined results on the economy will be highly beneficial.
"This is Pakistan's programme, not an IMF programme, but they would like to support it," he said.
Aziz said GDP growth in 1996/97 was unlikely to exceed four percent, roughly the same as in the past three years, but said he planned to raise it to six or seven percent in future.
He said the budget deficit would be "decisively" lower than last year's, but gave no precise estimate.
Aziz said the overall balance of payments gap could be around $3.5 billion, against $4 billion last year, a lower reduction than the previous government had promised.

He said a debt retirement scheme launched by Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif, under which Pakistanis may contribute gifts, interest-free loans or interest-bearing two-year deposits, would bolster Pakistan's liquid reserves, now at $1.15 billion.
The scheme has brought in about $200 million so far, mostly in two-year deposits, which Aziz compared to the $130 million which the next tranche of the standby loan would have provided.
"Therefore the balance of payments position will be slightly better, not totally comfortable, but slightly better," he said.

Aziz said the government would announce an industrial revival package in the next few days, to be followed by a similar package for agriculture early in April. "There is a need for tariff reform to reduce the incidence of tariffs on the economy and expose it to greater competition," he said. "There is a need to reduce the rate of personal and corporate taxes so that investment is encouraged."
He said exports must grow 20 to 25 percent over the next three years or "all these solutions will prove irrelevant".
Sharif's government took power last month after comfortably defeating ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party in February 3 elections.

"I must say that our reform programme has a better chance of producing good results because of the political stability that is now available and because of the perception of a business-friendly government," Aziz said. "

Pakistan started a three-year ESAF programme with the IMF in February 1994, but stopped it in June 1995. It began a standby loan later that year, but the IMF suspended it in April 1996. It was resumed by a caretaker government in December.
